sources.author: Irfan Habib

claims.note: The Mamluk sultans held the Doab and the Punjab. Expansion south comes later.
Khalji and early Tughlaq maximum. Gujarat taken 1299. Southern conquests were raids and short-lived tributary arrangements rather than settled territory, so they are not drawn as held.
Contraction under the later Tughlaqs. Bengal gone 1352, the Deccan gone 1347, Gujarat and Malwa going.
After Timur sacked Delhi in 1398 the sultanate held little beyond the Doab and the Punjab. The Sayyids and Lodis ruled from there until Panipat.
The peninsula south of the Krishna and Tungabhadra. The doab between the two rivers was contested with the Bahmanis throughout and is not separately drawn.

After Talikota the empire survived at Penukonda and Chandragiri with its nayakas increasingly independent. Drawn as the same ground because the successor nayaka states are not yet modelled separately.
Broke from Delhi in 1347 and held the Deccan between the Krishna and the Tapti until the five successor sultanates divided it.
Independent of Delhi from Ilyas Shah's unification until the Mughal conquest.
Zafar Khan governed independently from 1391 and took the title of sultan in 1407.
Babur and Humayun held the Doab and the Punjab, and Humayun lost even that to Sher Shah between 1540 and 1555.
Akbar's empire: Gujarat 1573, Bengal 1576, the whole northern plain.
The Deccan sultanates annexed under Aurangzeb — Bijapur 1686, Golconda 1687. The far south was never held.
